title: Comparing Fractions
topic: Comparing fractions with the same and different denominators
description: A short example course, and a template for contributors. Two lessons: comparing fractions that share a denominator, then fractions that do not, finished with a number line you build by hand.
author: Well of Wisdom contributors

lessons.title: Same denominator
lessons.summary: When the bottom numbers match, compare the top numbers.

content.title: Same size pieces
content.body:
The bottom number of a fraction, the **denominator**, says how many equal pieces the whole is cut into. The top number, the **numerator**, says how many of those pieces you have.

When two fractions have the same denominator, the pieces are the same size. So the fraction with more pieces is bigger: $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$, because five eighths is more than three eighths.

- Same denominator: compare the numerators.
- The bigger numerator is the bigger fraction.

content.explanation: The pieces are the same size (eighths), and 5 pieces is more than 3 pieces.
content.hint: Both are cut into eighths. Who has more pieces?

content.prompt: How many eighths make one whole?
content.explanation: A whole cut into eighths has 8 pieces, so $\frac{8}{8} = 1$.
content.hint: Count the pieces in a pizza cut into eighths.

lessons.title: Different denominators
lessons.summary: Rename the fractions so the pieces are the same size, then compare.

content.title: Making the pieces match
content.body:
Thirds and fifths are different sized pieces, so you cannot compare $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{3}{5}$ just by looking at the tops.

Find a denominator both can become. Fifteen works, because $3 \times 5 = 15$.

- $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{10}{15}$ (multiply top and bottom by 5)
- $\frac{3}{5} = \frac{9}{15}$ (multiply top and bottom by 3)

Now the pieces match, and 10 fifteenths is more than 9 fifteenths, so $\frac{2}{3} > \frac{3}{5}$.

content.prompt: Write $\frac{3}{4}$ with a denominator of 12. What is the new numerator?
content.explanation: Multiply the top and bottom by 3: $\frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{12}$.
content.hint: What do you multiply 4 by to get 12?

content.answer: Rename one half as two quarters. Two quarters is less than three quarters, so one half is less than three quarters.
content.explanation: Any explanation that makes the pieces the same size first is a good one.

content.title: A fraction number line
content.description: Draw a line from 0 to 1 on a long strip of paper. Mark halves, quarters and eighths on it, each in its own colour. Then place $\frac{3}{8}$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ on the line and write one sentence about what the line shows you.
content.rubric:
- Halves, quarters and eighths are each evenly spaced
- The three fractions sit in the right places
- The sentence uses the line to compare at least two fractions
